farraa:1-1.t:
I said: what do you think of what comes in the nominative after the letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf al-hijāʾ), such as His saying: ﴿المص كتابٌ أنزل إِليك﴾, and His saying: ﴿الم تنزِيلُ الكتابِ﴾, and His saying: ﴿الر كِتابٌ أحكمت آياتهُ﴾, and the like — by what did you put الكتاب in the nominative in these passages? I said: I put it in the nominative by the letters of the alphabet that precede it; as though you said: alif, lām, mīm and ṣād, of the disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa), are a Book sent down to you, assembled. If you say: it is as though you have made alif, lām, mīm and ṣād stand for all the letters of the alphabet, while they are three or four letters? I say: yes, just as you say: "ا ب ت ث are twenty-eight letters", contenting yourself with four letters out of twenty-eight. If you say: the alif of "ب ت ث" has become like a name for the letters of the alphabet, just as you say "I read al-Ḥamd", and it has become a name for the Opening of the Book. I say: what you say might come to mind, but you may say: "my son is in ا ب ت ث" [i.e. learning his letters], and if you said "in حاط" it would be permissible, and you would know that he means: my son is at the disjointed letters.
Since one can make do with something other than their beginning, we know that their beginning is not a name for them, even though their beginning is more favoured in mention than the rest of them. If you say: then how did the letters of (المص) and (كهيعص) come out of order and yet are treated like "bā tā thā", which are consecutive? I say: when they are mentioned consecutively they indicate ا ب ت ث themselves, disjointed; and when they do not come consecutively they indicate connected speech, not the disjointed letters.
Al-Ḥārithī recited to me:
تعلمت باجاد وآل مُرامِرٍ * وسوّدتُ أثوابى ولست بكاتب
(I learned "Bā-Jād" and the family of Murāmir, and blackened my clothes [with ink], yet I am no scribe.)
And one of the Banū Asad recited to me:
لّما رأيت أمرها فى حُطِّى * وفَنَكت فى كذب ولط أخذتُ منها بقرونٍ شُمطِ * ولم يزل ضربى لها ومَعْطِى * حتى على الرأسِ دم يغطِى
(When I saw her affair was at "Ḥuṭṭī", and she persisted in lying and deceit, I seized her by grey-streaked locks, and my beating and plucking of her did not cease until blood covered the head.)
So he contented himself with Ḥuṭṭī for Abū Jād. And if someone said: "the boy is at Hawwaz" or "Kalaman", that would suffice for Abū Jād.
Al-Kisāʾī said: I put ﴿كتابٌ أنزل إليك﴾ and similar nominatives after the letters in the nominative by implying (هذا) "this" or (ذلك) "that"; and that is a valid view. It is as though, when he implies (هذا) or (ذلك), he implies for the letters of the alphabet something before them that puts them in the nominative; because they must have a grammatical position.
He said: then what do you think of those of them after which comes nothing that pairs with them in the nominative (yurāfiʿuhu), such as His saying: حم. عسق, and يس, and ق, and ص, few or many — what is its position, since there is no nominative partner after it? I said: before it there is an implied pronoun that puts it in the nominative, like the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿براءة مِن اللّهِ ورسولِهِ﴾, the meaning being, and Allah knows best: this is an immunity from Allah. Likewise ﴿سورة أَنزلناها﴾. And likewise every nominative word with "saying" where you see nothing with it that puts it in the nominative: before it there is an implied noun that puts it in the nominative; such as His saying: ﴿ولا تقولوا ثلاثة انتهوا﴾, the meaning being, and Allah knows best: do not say "they are three", meaning the gods. Likewise His saying: ﴿سيقولون ثلاثة رابِعهم﴾, the meaning being, and Allah knows best: they will say: "they are three".
It has been said about (كهيعص) that it is an explanation of names of Allah: it is said the kāf is from Karīm, the hāʾ from Hādī, the ʿayn and the yāʾ from ʿAlīm, and the ṣād from Ṣadūq. If it is so, then (الذكر) is in the nominative by an implied pronoun, not by (كهيعص). And it has been said about (طه) that it means "O man"; if it is so, it does not need a nominative partner, because the one addressed in the vocative is in the nominative by the vocative. Likewise (يس): it has come that it means "O human", and some say "O man"; and the explanation of it is like the explanation of طه.
[Translator's note: the entry opens with "قلت" ("I said") where the question would be expected to begin "فإن قلت" ("if you say"); translated as written.]

farraa:2-2.t:
His saying: ﴿فَلاَ يَكُنْ فِي صَدْرِكَ حَرَجٌ مِّنْهُ﴾: He says: let your breast not be constricted by the Qurʾān through their calling you a liar; and as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿فلعلك باخِع نفسك على آثارِهِم إِن لم يؤمِنوا﴾. And it has been said: ﴿فلا يكن فى صدرك حرج﴾: doubt.
﴿لِتُنذِرَ بِهِ﴾ is placed later, and its meaning is: Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād, a Book sent down to you that you may warn by it, so let there be no constriction in your breast from it.
﴿وَذِكْرَىٰ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ is in the position of the accusative and the nominative. If you wish you may put it in the nominative, referring it back to الكتاب, as though you said: a true Book and a reminder for the believers; and the accusative means: that you may warn and remind the believers by it.

farraa:3-3.t:
His saying: ﴿ٱتَّبِعُواْ مَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ﴾: He addressed the Prophet ﷺ alone only because whatever he was warned with, his community was warned with; as He said: ﴿يأيها النبِىّ إِذا طلقتم النِساء﴾: He addressed him, then made the verb belong to all. And you may say to a man: "Woe to you, do you [plural] not fear Allah?", meaning him and his household or his clan. And His saying (اتبِعوا) may be reported speech from His saying (لتنذر به), because warning is speech; as though it were said to him: that you may say to them: "follow"; as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿يوصِيكم الله فِى أولادِكم للذكرِ مِثل حظِّ الأنثيينِ﴾, because enjoining is speech.
Similar to it: ﴿يأيها النبِىُّ لِم تحرِّم ما أحلَّ الله لك﴾, then He said: ﴿قد فرض الله لكم﴾, using the plural.

farraa:4-4.t:
His saying: ﴿وَكَم مِّن قَرْيَةٍ أَهْلَكْنَاهَا فَجَآءَهَا﴾: it may be said: the calamity came to it only before the destruction, so how is the destruction put first? I said: because the destruction and the calamity occur together; as you say: "أعطيتنى فأحسنت" ("you gave to me and did well"), and the doing well was not after the giving nor before it; they occurred together only, so that was considered permissible. And if you wish, the meaning may be: how many a town We destroyed, and the coming of the calamity was before the destruction, so you implied kāna.
That was permissible only on a meaning resembling this; and in conditional-type sequences that follow a known antecedent it is not possible to put the later first or the earlier last; as in your saying "ضربته فبكى" ("I struck him and he wept") and "أعطيته فاستغنى" ("I gave to him and he became rich") — unless you leave the words in their places. And His saying ﴿أَهْلَكْنَاهَا فَجَآءَهَا﴾ may be two statements as with wāw: We destroyed it, and the calamity came to it by night.
His saying: ﴿أَوْ هُمْ قَآئِلُونَ﴾: He referred the verb back to the people of the town, while at its beginning He said (أهلكناها) and did not say "We destroyed them and it came to them"; and if it had been said, it would be correct. And He did not say قائلة; and if it had been said, it would be correct.
His saying: ﴿أَوْ هُمْ قَآئِلُونَ﴾: a wāw is implied. The meaning is: We destroyed it and Our calamity came to it by night, or while they were taking their midday rest; they found one conjunction upon another heavy; but if it were said it would be permissible; as you say in speech: "أتيتنى واليا، أو وأنا معزول" ("you came to me when I was governor, or when I was dismissed"); and if you say "أو أنا معزول", you are implying the wāw.

farraa:5-5.t:
His saying: ﴿فَمَا كَانَ دَعْوَاهُمْ﴾: الدعوى is in the position of the accusative for kāna, and the nominative of kāna is His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ أَن قَالُوۤاْ﴾, so أن is in the position of the nominative. That is the way in most of the Qurʾān: when أن has a verb with it, it is made nominative and the [other] noun accusative; such as His saying: ﴿فكان عاقِبتَهما أنهما فِى النار﴾ and ﴿ما كان حجتهم إِلا أن قالوا﴾. And if you made الدعوى nominative (and أن) in the position of the accusative, it would be correct; as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿ليس البرُّ أن تُولوا﴾, and in one of the two readings it is: ليس البر بأن تولوا.
[Translator's note: "and the verb accusative (والفعل منصوبا)" in the source; al-Farrāʾ means the noun paired with kāna, i.e. its predicate.]

farraa:8-8.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلْوَزْنُ يَوْمَئِذٍ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾: if you wish you may put الوزن in the nominative by الحقّ [as its predicate], and that is the natural form of the speech. And if you wish you may put الوزن in the nominative by يومئذ, as though you said: the weighing on the Day of Resurrection is truly (حقّاً), putting الحقّ in the accusative even though it has alif and lām; as He said: ﴿فالحقَّ والحقَّ أقول﴾: the first is accusative by something other than أقول.
And the second by أقول.
His saying: ﴿فَمَن ثَقُلَتْ مَوَازِينُهُ فَأُوْلَـٰئِكَ﴾: He did not say (فذلك), making it singular because مَن is singular; and if He had made it singular it would be correct. And (مَن) can be taken to refer to one or to many.
And that is common.

farraa:10-10.t: His saying: ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا لَكُمْ فِيهَا مَعَايِشَ﴾: it is not pronounced with hamza, because it — I mean the singular — is of the pattern mafʿila, the yāʾ being part of the root; therefore it is not given hamza. What is given hamza of this kind is only where the yāʾ is an added letter, such as madīna and madāʾin, and qabīla and qabāʾil: since the yāʾ had no known root and then an anonymous alif was also joined to it, it was given hamza. And like maʿāyish among those from wāw roots which are not given hamza if you form the plural: maʿūna, you say (معاون); or manāra, you say manāwir. That is because the wāw returns to its original form, the alif before it being quiescent. Sometimes the Arabs give hamza to this and its like, imagining that it is of the pattern faʿīla because it resembles that pattern in pronunciation and in the number of letters; just as they made the plural of masīl al-māʾ (watercourse) amsila, likening it to faʿīl, while it is mafʿil. And the Arabs have given hamza to al-maṣāʾib, whose singular is muṣība, likening it to faʿīla because of its frequency in speech.

farraa:12-12.t:
His saying: ﴿قَالَ مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلاَّ تَسْجُدَ﴾: the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: what prevented you from prostrating. And (أن) in this place is accompanied by لا, and (لا) is a ṣila (redundant connective). That is done with whatever has a negation at its beginning. And sometimes they repeat a negation on its predicate to make the negation firm and emphasise it; as they said:
ما إن رأينا مثلهن لمعشر * سود الرءوس فوالج وفيول
(Never have we seen the like of them belonging to any people of black heads: camels and elephants.)
(ما) is a negation and (إن) is a negation, and they were combined for emphasis. Similar to it: ﴿وما يشعِركم أنها إذا جاءت لا يؤمِنون﴾. And similar to it: ﴿وحرام على قريةٍ أهلكناها أنهم لا يرجِعون﴾. And similar to it: ﴿لئلا يعلم أهل الكتاب ألا يقدرون﴾, except that the meaning of the dropped negation in لئلا is from its beginning, not from its end; the meaning is: that the People of the Book may know that they have no power.
His saying: ﴿مَا مَنَعَكَ﴾: (ما) is in the position of the nominative. And if a properly formed answer were given to its like in speech, it would be nominative; you would say: "منعنى منك أنك بخيل" ("what prevented me from you is that you are stingy"). And this is one of those whose answer is given not on the structure of its beginning; for he said: ﴿أَنَاْ خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ﴾, and did not say: "what prevented me from prostrating is that I am better than him"; as you say in speech: "How did you spend the night?" and he says: "صالح" ("well"), in the nominative; or you say: "أنا بخير" ("I am well"), and infer from it the meaning of the answer. If the answer were properly formed he would say صالحا, i.e. I spent the night well.

farraa:16-16.t: His saying: ﴿لأَقْعُدَنَّ لَهُمْ صِرَاطَكَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾: the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: I will surely sit in wait for them on their path or in their path. Dropping the ṣifa (preposition) in this is permissible; as one says: "قعدت لك وجه الطريق" and "على وجه الطريق" ("I sat waiting for you at the face of the road"); because الطريق is a locative in meaning, so it bears what "the day", "the night" and "the year" bear when it is said: "آتيك غدا" or "آتيك فى غد" ("I will come to you tomorrow").

farraa:26-26.t:
His saying: ﴿يَابَنِيۤ ءَادَمَ قَدْ أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكُمْ لِبَاساً يُوَارِي سَوْءَاتِكُمْ وَرِيشاً﴾, [also read] "ورياشا". If you wish you may make riyāsh a plural whose singular is rīsh; and if you wish you may make riyāsh a maṣdar in the sense of rīsh, as one says libs and libās; the poet said:
فلما كشفن اللِّبْسَ عنه مَسَحْنَه * بأطراف طَفْلٍ زان غَيْلا مُوَشَّما
(When they uncovered the garment from it, they stroked it with soft fingertips that adorned a plump, tattooed forearm.)
His saying: ﴿ورِيشاً ولِباسُ التقوى﴾ and "لباسَ التقوى": it is put in the nominative by His saying "and the garment of piety is better", and (ذلك) is made part of its description. In the reading of both Ubayy and ʿAbdallāh it is: "ولباس التقوى خير". In our reading it is (ذلك خير), so the accusative of اللباس is dearer to me, because it follows الريش, (ذلك خير): خير is put in the nominative by ذلك.

farraa:29-29.t:
His saying: ﴿ كَمَا بَدَأَكُمْ تَعُودُونَ﴾: He says: He began you in creation wretched and happy, so likewise you will return to wretchedness and happiness.
His saying: ﴿وَأَقِيمُواْ وُجُوهَكُمْ عِندَ كُلِّ مَسْجِدٍ﴾: He says: when the prayer overtakes you while you are at a mosque, pray in it, and do not say: "I will go to the mosque of my people." If it is outside the time of prayer, you pray wherever you wish.

farraa:30-30.t: His saying: ﴿فَرِيقاً هَدَىٰ وَفَرِيقاً حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلضَّلاَلَةُ﴾: الفريق is put in the accusative by تعودون [Translator's note: the source has "بتعذون", evidently a misprint for بتعودون], and in the reading of Ubayy it is: "تعودون فريقين فريقا هدى وفريقا حقَّ عليهم الضلالة". If both were nominative it would be correct; as He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿كان لكم آيةٌ فى فِئَتْينِ التقتا فِئةٌ تقاتِلُ فى سبِيل اللّهِ وأُخرى كافِرةٌ﴾ and "فِئَةً"; and similar to it: ﴿وتُنذِرَ يوم الجمعِ لا ريب فِيهِ فرِيقٌ فى الجنةِ وفرِيقٌ فى السَّعِير﴾. And the [first] فريق may be accusative because "هَدَى" falls on it, and the second accusative by a verb falling on a pronoun referring back to it; like His saying: ﴿يدخِل من يشاء فى رحمتِهِ والظالِمين أَعدَّ لهم عذاباً أَلِيماً﴾.

farraa:32-32.t:
His saying: ﴿قُلْ هِي لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ فِي ٱلْحَيَاةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا خَالِصَةً يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَامَةِ﴾: you put خالصة in the accusative by qaṭʿ (cutting off), and you made the predicate lie in the lām of الذين; but al-khāliṣa is not cut off from that lām, rather it is cut off from another, implied lām. The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: say: it is for those who believe in the life of this world — He means shared — and it is theirs exclusively in the Hereafter.
If you put it in the nominative it would be correct, referring it back to the position of the ṣifa (prepositional phrase) by which it was put in the nominative, since that is in the position of the nominative.
Similar to it in speech is someone's saying: "إنا بخير كثير صيدنا" ("we are well, our game plentiful"). And similar to it is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إِن الإنسان خُلِق هَلوعا. إِذا مسّه الشرّ جَزوعا. وإذا مسّه الخير منوعا﴾. The meaning: he was created anxious; then He explained the state of the anxious one in the accusative, because it was accusative at the beginning of the speech. If it were put in the nominative it would be permissible; except that its nominative would be by resumption (istiʾnāf), because there is no prepositional phrase with it to put it in the nominative.
This verse was revealed only because tribes of the Arabs in the Jāhiliyya used to eat nothing in the days of their pilgrimage but bare sustenance, and would not eat meat or fat; and they would circumambulate the House naked, the men by day and the women by night; and a woman would wear something like the ḥawf (a strip-skirt) to cover her somewhat. Therefore the ʿĀmirī woman said:
اليوم يبدو بعضه أو كله * وما بدا منه فلا أُحله
(Today some or all of it shows; and whatever of it shows, I do not make it lawful.)
The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have more right to exert ourselves for our Lord", and they wanted to do as the people of the Jāhiliyya did; so Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent down: ﴿خذوا زِينتكم عِند كل مسجِدٍ﴾, meaning clothing; ﴿وكلوا واشربوا ولا تسرفوا﴾ so far that it leads you to forbid what I have made lawful for you; and extravagance (al-isrāf) here is excess in religion.

farraa:33-33.t: His saying: ﴿قُلْ إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ رَبِّيَ ٱلْفَوَاحِشَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ وَٱلإِثْمَ﴾: (والإثم) is what falls short of a ḥadd (prescribed penalty); (والبغى) is overbearing against people.

farraa:37-37.t:
His saying: ﴿أُوْلَـٰئِكَ يَنَالُهُمْ نَصِيبُهُم مِّنَ ٱلْكِتَابِ﴾: it is said: what Allah decreed against them in the Book will reach them: blackness of faces and blueness of eyes.
That is His saying: ﴿ويوم القِيامةِ ترى الذِين كذبوا على الله وجوههم مسودة﴾. And it is said: it is the punishment that reaches them in this world short of the punishment of the Hereafter, so that it is from His saying: ﴿ولنذِيقنهم مِن العذابِ الأدنى دون العذابِ الأكبر﴾.

farraa:38-38.t: His saying: ﴿كُلَّمَا دَخَلَتْ أُمَّةٌ لَّعَنَتْ أُخْتَهَا﴾: He says: the one that preceded it, and it is its sister in its religion, not in lineage. As for His saying: ﴿وإلى مدين أخاهم شعيبا﴾, he was not their brother in their religion, but he was one of them.

farraa:40-40.t:
His saying: ﴿لاَ تُفَتَّحُ لَهُمْ﴾, and لا يَفتَّح and تُفَتَّح. Masculine and feminine are permissible with the plural only because the feminine applies to it, so both forms are permissible in it; as He said: ﴿يوم تشهد عليهم ألسنتهم﴾ and "يشهد". Whoever uses the masculine says: the singular of الألسنة is masculine, so I build on the singular, since the verb is singular when it precedes plural nouns, as you say: ذهب القوم ("the people went").
Sometimes the Readers prefer one of the two forms, or it comes in the Book in one form, and someone who does not know thinks that nothing else is permissible, while it is permissible. Among cases where they preferred the feminine is His saying: ﴿يوم تبيض وجوه وتسود وجوه﴾: they preferred the feminine. Among cases where they preferred the masculine is His saying: ﴿لن ينال الله لحومها ولا دِماؤها﴾. And what came in the Book in one of the two forms is His saying: ﴿فتِحت أبوابها﴾; if it had come in the masculine it would be correct.
The meaning of His saying: ﴿لاَ تُفَتَّحُ لَهُمْ أَبْوَابُ ٱلسَّمَآءِ﴾ is: their deeds do not ascend. And it is said that the deeds of the wicked do not ascend but are written on a rock beneath the earth, and that is what Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿كلا إِن كِتاب الفجارِ لفِى سجين﴾.
His saying: ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَلِجَ ٱلْجَمَلُ فِي سَمِّ ٱلْخِيَاطِ﴾: al-jamal is the mate of the she-camel. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: al-jummal, meaning ropes bound together. One says al-khiyāṭ and al-mikhyaṭ, meaning the needle. In the reading of ʿAbdallāh it is (المِخْيَط); and the like comes on these two patterns; one says: izār and miʾzar, liḥāf and milḥaf, qināʿ and miqnaʿ, qirām and miqram.

farraa:48-48.t: His saying: ﴿وَنَادَىٰ أَصْحَابُ ٱلأَعْرَافِ رِجَالاً يَعْرِفُونَهُمْ بِسِيمَاهُمْ﴾: that is because they are on a wall between Paradise and the Fire called al-Aʿrāf; they see the people of Paradise and recognise them by the whiteness of their faces, and they recognise the people of the Fire by the blackness of their faces. That is His saying: ﴿يعرِفون كلا بسيماهم﴾. The people of al-Aʿrāf are folk whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal; their good deeds fell short of bringing them to Paradise, and their bad deeds did not bring them to the Fire. They were held back, then Allah admitted them to Paradise by the grace of His mercy.

farraa:52-52.t: His saying: ﴿ وَلَقَدْ جِئْنَاهُمْ بِكِتَابٍ فَصَّلْنَاهُ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍ هُدًى وَرَحْمَةً﴾: you put "guidance" and "mercy" in the accusative by qaṭʿ (cutting off) from the hāʾ in فصّلناه. And you may put them in the accusative by the verb. If you put it in the genitive as following الكتاب it would be correct; as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿وهذا كِتاب أنزلناه مبارك﴾, making it nominative by its following الكتاب.

farraa:53-53.t:
His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلاَّ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾: the hāʾ in تأويله is for the Book. He means its outcome and what Allah promised in it.
His saying: ﴿فَهَل لَّنَا مِن شُفَعَآءَ فَيَشْفَعُواْ لَنَآ أَوْ نُرَدُّ﴾: it is not conjoined to (فيشفعوا); the meaning — and Allah knows best — is only: or will we be returned, so that we do other than what we used to do.
And if you put (نردّ) in the accusative by making (أو) equivalent to حتّى, it would be as though he said: so that they intercede for us forever until we are returned and do [otherwise]; but we know of no reader who read it so.

farraa:56-56.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّ رَحْمَتَ ٱللَّهِ قَرِيبٌ مِّنَ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾: He made قريب masculine because it is not kinship in lineage. He said: I have observed that the Arabs make al-qarība (a female relative) in lineage feminine, without disagreement; but when they say "دارك منّا قريب" ("your house is near us") or "فلانة منك قريب" ("so-and-so [fem.] is near you"), in nearness and distance, they use both masculine and feminine. That is because al-qarīb in meaning, even though it is nominative, is as it were in the sense of: it is from a near place. So al-qarīb is made a substitute for "place"; as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿وما هِى مِن الظالِمِين ببعِيد﴾, and said: ﴿وما يدرِيك لعل الساعة تكون قريبا﴾. If one made that feminine, building on "it became distant from you, so it is distant (بعيدة)" and "it became near, so it is near (قريبة)", it would be correct and good. ʿUrwa said:
عشِيَّةَ لاعفراءُ مِنك قرِيبة * فتدنو ولا عفراء مِنك بعِيد
(On the evening when ʿAfrāʾ is neither near you, so that she might draw close, nor is ʿAfrāʾ far from you.)
Whoever uses the nominative with the masculine does not make قريب plural [and does not] make it dual. And whoever says "إنّ عفراء منك قريبة أو بعيدة" makes it dual and plural.

farraa:57-57.t:
His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِي يُرْسِلُ ٱلرِّيَاحَ نَشْراً﴾: al-nashr among the winds is the pleasant, gentle one that raises clouds. The companions of ʿAbdallāh read it so. Others read (بُشْرا). Muḥammad narrated to us, he said: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us, he said: Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ al-Asadī narrated to me from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī from Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī from ʿAlī that he read (بُشْرا), meaning bearing good news (bashīra); and (بَشْرا), like the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: (يرسل الرياح مبشِّرات).
His saying: ﴿فَأَنْزَلْنَا بِهِ ٱلْمَآءَ فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِ مِن كُلِّ ٱلثَّمَرَاتِ كَذٰلِكَ نُخْرِجُ ٱلْموْتَىٰ﴾: "We brought forth by it" is a response to "We sent down". It is said that people and all creatures die at the first blowing [of the Trumpet], and between it and the last are forty years. Allah sends rain, and it rains for forty days like the semen of men, and they grow in their graves as they grow in their mothers' bellies. That is His saying: ﴿كَذٰلِكَ نُخْرِجُ ٱلْموْتَىٰ﴾: as We brought forth the fruits from the dead earth.

farraa:58-58.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱلَّذِي خَبُثَ لاَ يَخْرُجُ إِلاَّ نَكِداً﴾ is the reading of the generality; and some of the people of Medina read نَكَدا, meaning: it comes out only in scantiness (nakad).
Nakid and nakad are like danif and danaf. He said: and I would not rule out that there is a form nakud in it, though I have not heard it; but I have heard ḥadhir and ḥadhur, ashir and ashur, ʿajil and ʿajul.

farraa:59-59.t:
His saying: ﴿مَا لَكُمْ مِّنْ إِلَـٰهٍ غَيْرُهُ﴾: you make (غير) a naʿt (adjective) of إله [in the genitive]. And it may be put in the nominative, made to follow the underlying sense of إله; do you not see that if you removed (مِن) from إله it would be nominative? It has been read in both ways.
Some of the Banū Asad and Quḍāʿa, when (غير) has the sense of (إلا), put it in the accusative, whether the speech before it is complete or not. So they say: "ما جاءنى غيرَك" ("none but you came to me") and "ما أتانى أحد غيرَك" ("no one came to me but you"). He said: al-Mufaḍḍal recited to me:
لم يمنع الشربَ منها غير ان هتفت * حمامةٌ من سَحُوقٍ ذاتِ أوقال
(Nothing kept her from drinking except that a dove cooed from a tall palm laden with fruit.)
This is accusative, and the verb belongs to it [as agent], the speech being incomplete. And another said:
لاعيب فيها غيرَ شُهْلةِ عينِها * كذاك عِتاق الطير شُهْلاً عيونُها
(There is no fault in her but the bluish-grey of her eye; thus are noble birds, grey-blue their eyes.)
This is accusative, and the speech before it is complete.

farraa:63-63.t:
His saying: ﴿أَوَ عَجِبْتُمْ﴾: this is a conjunctive wāw (wāw nasaq) on which the interrogative alif has been brought in, just as you bring it in on the fāʾ and say أفعجبتم; it is not أَوْ; if أَوْ were meant, the wāw would be quiescent.
His saying: ﴿أَوَ عَجِبْتُمْ أَن جَآءَكُمْ ذِكْرٌ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ عَلَىٰ رَجُلٍ﴾: it is said in the exegesis: with a man.
In speech it is like your saying: "جاءنا الخير على وجهك" ("good came to us at your face"), and "هُدِينا الخير على لسانك" ("we were guided to good on your tongue"), and "مع وجهك"; both are permissible.

farraa:65-65.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِلَىٰ عَادٍ أَخَاهُمْ هُوداً﴾
[Translator's note: the source entry consists only of this quotation, with no comment.]

farraa:66-66.t: His saying: ﴿قَالَ ٱلْمَلأُ﴾: they are men, among whom there is no woman. Likewise al-qawm, al-nafar and al-rahṭ.

farraa:68-68.t: His saying: ﴿وَأَنَاْ لَكُمْ نَاصِحٌ أَمِينٌ﴾: he says: I was trustworthy among you before I was sent. And it is said: trustworthy with the message.

farraa:100-100.t:
His saying: ﴿أَن لَّوْ نَشَآءُ أَصَبْنَاهُمْ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾, then He said: ﴿ونطبع﴾, and did not say "وطبعنا"; ونطبع is cut off from the apodosis (jawāb) of لو; what shows you that is His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَسْمَعُونَ﴾; do you not see that it is not permissible in speech to say "لو سألتنى لأعطيتك فأنت غنىّ" ("had you asked me I would have given to you, so you are rich"), until you say: "لو سألتنى لأعطيتك فاستغنيت" ("… and you would have become rich")? If the meaning in His saying ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَسْمَعُونَ﴾ allowed it to be connected with what precedes, it would be permissible to refer a yafʿal (imperfect) back to a faʿala (past) in the apodosis of لو; as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿ولو يعجل الله لِلناسِ الشر استِعجالهم بِالخيرِ لقضِى إليهم أجلهم فنذر الذِين لا يرجون﴾: فنذر is referred back to (لقضِى), and it has the nūn.
What made that easy is that the Arabs do not say وذرت or ودعت; one says it only with the yāʾ, alif, nūn and tāʾ [prefixes of the imperfect]; so it was preferred to faʿala where permissible. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿تبارك الذِى إن شاء جعل لك خيرا مِن ذلِك﴾, then said: ﴿ويجعل لك قصورا﴾. So when the apodosis of لو comes to you, you prefer (faʿala to yafʿal) in it; and if you say it with yafʿal it is permissible; and conjoining faʿala to yafʿal and yafʿal to faʿala is permissible, because the interpretation is like the interpretation of a conditional (al-jazāʾ).
[Translator's note: the source has "ينفعل"; the sense requires يفعل, translated accordingly.]

farraa:105-105.t: His saying: ﴿حَقِيقٌ عَلَى أَنْ لاَّ أَقُولَ﴾, and it is read: (حقيقٌ علىّ أن لا أقول). In the reading of ʿAbdallāh: (حقيق بأن لا أقول على الله); this is the proof of whoever read (على) and did not put it in construct with the first-person pronoun. The Arabs put the bāʾ in the place of على: "رميت على القوس" and "بالقوس" ("I shot with the bow"), and "جئت على حال حسنةٍ" and "بحال حسنةٍ" ("I came in a good state").

farraa:107-107.t: His saying: ﴿فَإِذَا هِيَ ثُعْبَانٌ﴾: it is the male serpent, and it is the greatest of snakes.

farraa:110-110.t:
His saying: ﴿ يُرِيدُ أَن يُخْرِجَكُمْ مِّنْ أَرْضِكُمْ فَمَاذَا تَأْمُرُونَ﴾: His saying ﴿يُرِيدُ أَن يُخْرِجَكُمْ مِّنْ أَرْضِكُمْ﴾ is from the chiefs, and ﴿فَمَاذَا تَأْمُرُونَ﴾ is from the speech of Pharaoh. That was permissible following their speech to him, as though it were not reported speech while it is reported speech. If you made the reporting explicit you would say: "he wants to drive you out of your land", and he said: "So what do you command?". Analogy allows you to say on this pattern: "قلت لجاريتك قومى فإنى قائمة" ("I said to your slave-girl: stand up — for I am standing") (meaning: and she said: I am standing). Its like seldom comes in poetry or elsewhere. ʿAntara said:
الشاتَمِىْ عِرْضى ولم أشتِمْهُما * والناذرَيْنِ إِذا لقيتهما دمى
(The two who revile my honour though I did not revile them, and who vow my blood when I meet them.)
This resembles that; because it is reported speech and has become as if connected, not as reported speech; do you not see that he meant: the two who vowed "if we meet ʿAntara we shall kill him", and he said "when I meet them", reporting about himself, whereas they had mentioned him in the third person. And the meaning of "I meet them" is: they meet me.

farraa:111-111.t:
His saying: ﴿أَرْجِهْ وَأَخَاهُ﴾: the exegesis has come: detain them both with you and do not kill them; and al-irjāʾ is postponing the matter. Ḥamza and al-Aʿmash made the hāʾ quiescent (jazm). It is a dialect of the Arabs: they pause on the pronominal hāʾ in continuous speech when what precedes it is vowelled. One of them recited to me:
أنحى علىَّ الدهر رجلا ويدا * يُقسم لا يُصلح إلا أفسدا * فيصلح اليوم ويفسدُهْ غدا
(Fate has turned on me foot and hand; it swears it mends nothing but it spoils it: it mends today and spoils it tomorrow.)
And likewise with the feminine hāʾ: they say "هذه طلحهْ قد أقبلت" ("this is Ṭalḥa, she has come"), with sukūn. One of them recited to me:
لما رأى أن لاّدعَهْ ولا شِبَعْ * مال إلى أرطاة حِقْف فاضطجع
(When he saw there was neither rest nor fill, he turned to an arṭā shrub of a sand-dune and lay down.)
And al-Qanānī recited to me:
لستُ إذاً لزَعْبَلَهْ إن لم أُغَـ * يِّرْ بِكْلَتِى إن لم أُساوَ بالطُوَل
(Then I am no [son] of Zaʿbala if I do not change my way, if I am not made equal with the tall ones.)
بِكْلَتِى: my way; as though he said: if I do not change my way until I am made equal. And this [الطُوَل] is for a woman: a tall woman (ṭūlā) and tall [women] (ṭuwal).

farraa:73-73.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِلَىٰ ثَمُودَ أَخَاهُمْ صَالِحاً﴾ is accusative by an implied "We sent (أرسلنا)". If it were put in the nominative, since the verb is absent, it would be correct; as He said: ﴿فبشرناها بإسحاق ومِن وراءِ إسحاق يعقوبُ﴾. He also said: ﴿فأخرجنا بِهِ ثمراتٍ مختلِفا ألوانها﴾, then said: ﴿ومِن الجِبالِ جُدَدٌ بِيض﴾: the proper form here is the nominative, because the mountains do not follow the vegetation or the fruits. And if you put it in the accusative by implying: We made for you (من الجِبال جددا بيضا), [it would be permissible]; as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿ختم الله على قلوبِهِم وعلى سمعِهِم وعلى أبصارِهم غشاوةً﴾ — one implies جَعَل for it when one reads the accusative; as He said: ﴿وختم على سمعِهِ وقلبِهِ وجعل على بصرِهِ غِشاوة﴾; but the nominative in غشاوة is the proper form. His saying: ﴿ومِن الناسِ والدوابِّ والأَنعامِ مختلِف ألوانه﴾: He did not say "their colours" (ألوانهم) or ألوانها. That is because of (مِن); the Arabs imply مَن and content themselves with مِن in place of مَن, saying: "مِنا مَنْ يقول ذلك ومِنا لا يقوله" ("of us is one who says that, and of us [one who] does not say it"). And if it were made plural according to the sense, it would be correct, as in the saying of Dhū al-Rumma:
فظلُّوا ومنهم دمعه سابق له * وآخر يثنِى دَمْعَة العينِ بالمَهلِ
(So they remained, one of them with his tears outrunning him, and another holding back the eye's tear with patience.)
His saying: ﴿وزادكم فىالخلقِ بسطة﴾: the tallest of them was a hundred cubits and the shortest sixty cubits.

farraa:78-78.t:
His saying: ﴿فَأَخَذَتْهُمُ ٱلرَّجْفَةُ﴾: al-rajfa is the earthquake, and al-ṣāʿiqa is the fire; it is said: it burnt them.
His saying: ﴿فَأَصْبَحُواْ فِي دَارِهِمْ جَاثِمِينَ﴾: He says: as crouching ashes.

farraa:79-79.t: His saying: ﴿فَتَوَلَّىٰ عَنْهُمْ﴾: it is said that He never punished a nation while its prophet was in it, until he left it.

farraa:82-82.t:
His saying: ﴿أَخْرِجُوهُمْ﴾ means Lot: expel him and his two daughters.
His saying: ﴿إِنَّهُمْ أُنَاسٌ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ﴾: they say: they shun the deeds of the people of Lot and keep themselves clean of them.

farraa:85-85.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُفْسِدُواْ فِي ٱلأَرْضِ بَعْدَ إِصْلاَحِهَا﴾: its setting right is the sending of the Prophet ﷺ, commanding the lawful and forbidding the unlawful.
That is its rightness. And its corruption is working acts of disobedience before the Prophet is sent.
The saying of Shuʿayb: ﴿قَدْ جَآءَتْكُمْ بَيِّنَةٌ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ﴾: he had no sign except prophethood. Thamūd had the she-camel, and Jesus had the raising of the dead and the like.

farraa:86-86.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تَقْعُدُواْ بِكُلِّ صِرَاطٍ تُوعِدُونَ﴾: they used to sit on their roads in wait for whoever believed in the Prophet, threatening them with death. It is al-īʿād and al-waʿīd (threat). When it is unspecified it is with alif [i.e. أوعد]; but when you make it take an object, saying "وعدتك خيرا أو شرا" ("I promised you good or evil"), it is without alif; as He, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿النارُ وعدها الله الذِين كفروا﴾.

farraa:89-89.t: His saying: ﴿رَبَّنَا ٱفْتَحْ بَيْنَنَا﴾ means: judge between us; the people of ʿUmān call the judge al-fātiḥ and al-fattāḥ.

farraa:115-115.t:
His saying: ﴿إِمَّآ أَن تُلْقِيَ وَإِمَّآ أَن نَّكُونَ نَحْنُ ٱلْمُلْقِينَ﴾: He brought (أن) in with (إما) because it is in the position of a command to choose. So it is in the position of the accusative, as in the saying "choose this or this"; do you not see that a command to choose would fit in the place of إمّا?
If you say: (أو) in meaning is equivalent to (إمّا … وإمّا), so may one say "يا زيد أن تقوم أو تقعد"? I say: that is not permissible; because with (أو) the first of the two nouns is a statement on which one may stop, then you add doubt about the other noun, continuing the speech on the statement; do you not see that you say "قام أخوك" ("your brother stood") and stop, and if it then occurs to you, you say "أو أبوك" ("or your father"), bringing in doubt, while the first noun is self-sufficient and one may stop on it. But it is not permissible to say "ضربت إمّا عبدالله" ("I struck either ʿAbdallāh") and stop. So since (إمّا) announces choice from the beginning of the speech, you introduced أن for it.
And if إمّا … وإمّا occur with two verbs that are connected with a definite or indefinite noun, and a command to distinguish does not fit in the place of إمّا, أن is not introduced in it; as in the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿وآخَرُون مُرْجَون لأَمْرِ الله إمَّّّا يعذِّبُهم وإمَّا يَتُوب عَلَيْهِمْ﴾; do you not see that a command is not fit here, therefore there is no أن in it. But if you made (أن) have the sense of (كى) and made it a ṣila (complement) of (مرجون), meaning "they were deferred to be punished or forgiven", that is fit with every complete verb, but not with kāna and its sisters nor with ẓanantu and its sisters. Of that is your saying: "آتيك إما أن تعطى وإما أن تمنع" ("I come to you, either that you give or that you refuse").
And it is a mistake to say "أظنك إما أن تعطى وإما أن تمنع", nor "أصبحت إما أن تعطى وإما أن تمنع". And do not bring (أو) in on (إما), nor (إما) on (أو). Sometimes the Arabs do that because of their kinship in meaning, by way of tawahhum (assumed construction); they say: "عبدالله إما جالس أو ناهض" ("ʿAbdallāh is either sitting or rising"), and they say: "عبدالله يقوم وإما يقعد". In the reading of Ubayy: (وإنا وإيَّاكم لإمَّا على هدى أو فى ضلال), putting أو in the place of إما. And the poet said:
فقلت لهن امشين إِمَّا نلاقِه * كما قال أو نشف النفوس فنعذرا
(I said to them: walk on — either we meet him as he said, or we heal our souls and are excused.)
And another said:
فكيف بنفس كلما قلت أشرفت * على البرء من دهماء هِيض اندمالها
تُهاض بدارٍ قد تقادم عهدُها * وإمّا بأمواتٍ ألمَّ خيالها
(How is it with a soul which, whenever I say it is nearing recovery from Dahmāʾ, its healing is broken again — broken anew by an abode long abandoned, or by the dead whose phantom visits?)
So he put (وإمّا) in the place of (أو). That is by tawahhum: when the expression is somewhat long, or you separate the two by something, then tawahhum is permissible; as you say: "أنت ضاربُ زيدٍ ظالما وأخاه" ("you are striking Zayd wrongfully, and his brother"): when you separated them by (ظالم), the accusative of الأخ was permissible though what preceded it is genitive. Similar to it: ﴿يا ذَا القَرْنَيْنِ إِمَّا أَنْ تُعَذِّبَ وإِمَّا أَنْ تَتَّخِذَ فِيهم حُسْناً﴾, and likewise His saying ﴿إِمَّا أنْ تُلْقِىَ وإِمَّا أَن نَّكُونَ أَوَّلَ مَنْ أَلْقَى﴾.

farraa:117-117.t: His saying: ﴿تَلْقَفُ مَا يَأْفِكُونَ﴾ and (تَلَقَّفُ). One says: لقِفت الشىء فأنا ألقفه لقفا ("I snatched the thing, I snatch it"); they make its maṣdar laqafān. In the exegesis it means: it swallows.

farraa:118-118.t: His saying: ﴿فَوَقَعَ ٱلْحَقُّ﴾: its meaning is that the sorcerers said: "If what Moses made were sorcery, our ropes and staffs would have returned to their former state; but they have vanished." That is His saying (فوقع الحق): the truth became clear from the sorcery.

farraa:123-123.t: His saying: ﴿آمَنتُمْ بِهِ﴾: he says: you believed him. And whoever says (آمنتم له) means: you granted him what he wanted.

farraa:124-124.t: His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ لأُصَلِّبَنَّكُمْ﴾ with doubling, and (لأَصْلِبنَّكم) without doubling, as some of the people of Mecca read it. It is like your saying: قتلت القوم and قتَّلتهم ("I killed the people"); when the killing is widespread, the doubled form is permissible.

farraa:127-127.t: His saying: ﴿وَيَذَرَكَ وَآلِهَتَكَ﴾: you have the accusative in (ويذرك) by al-ṣarf (diversion) [Translator's note: the Kufan term for the subjunctive after wāw of accompaniment]; because in the reading of Ubayy it is (أتذر موسى وقومه لِيفسِدوا فِى الأرض وقد تركوك أن يعبدوك); this is the meaning of al-ṣarf. And the nominative is for whoever makes the end of the speech follow its beginning; as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿من ذا الذِى يُقْرِضُ اللّهَ قَرْضاً حَسَناً فَيُضَاعِفه﴾ with the nominative. Ibn ʿAbbās read (وإلاهتك) and explained it: and leave you and the worship of you; and he said: Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship.

farraa:129-129.t: His saying: ﴿أُوذِينَا مِن قَبْلِ أَن تَأْتِينَا وَمِن بَعْدِ مَا جِئْتَنَا﴾: He said: as for the first harm, it was his killing the sons and sparing the women. Then, when they said to him: "Will you leave Moses and his people to work corruption in the land?", he said: "I will resume killing their sons and sparing the women as I did before." That is harm after the coming of Moses.

farraa:130-130.t: His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ أَخَذْنَآ آلَ فِرْعَونَ بِٱلسِّنِينَ﴾: He seized them with the years: drought and barrenness, year after year.

farraa:131-131.t:
His saying: ﴿فَإِذَا جَآءَتْهُمُ ٱلْحَسَنَةُ قَالُواْ لَنَا هَـٰذِهِ﴾: al-ḥasana here is al-khafḍ [Translator's note: so in the source; probably a misprint for الخِصْب, "fertility/plenty", the counterpart of الجدوبة below].
His saying: ﴿لَنَا هَـٰذِهِ﴾: they say: we deserve it. ﴿وَإِن تُصِبْهُمْ سَيِّئَةٌ﴾ means barrenness; (يّطّيروا) they take an evil omen (بِموسى) from Moses, as the Jews took an evil omen from the Prophet ﷺ in Medina, and said: "Our prices have risen and our rains have lessened since he came to us."

farraa:133-133.t: His saying: ﴿فَأَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلطُّوفَانَ﴾: Allah sent the sky upon them for a week, and it did not let up night or day, so the earth became narrow for them from the collapse of their houses and their being kept from their estates. They asked him [Moses] to remove it from them, and it was removed, but they did not repent. So Allah sent (الجراد) the locusts upon them, and they ate what the earth had grown in that year. That was because after that rain they saw a fertility the like of which they had never seen, and they said: "This was only a mercy for us, not a punishment." They were distressed by the locusts, which were a cubit deep on the ground, so they asked him to remove them from them and they would believe. Allah removed them, and there remained for them what they could eat; so they became arrogant by it and said (لن نؤمِن لك). Then Allah sent upon them (القمل), which is the wingless young locusts, and they ate all that the locusts had left; but they did not believe. So Allah sent (الضفادع) the frogs, and one of them would wake on his bed with them piled up; they were distressed by that, and when it was removed from them they did not believe. So Allah sent upon them (الدم) the blood: their springs and their rivers turned to blood until the first-born died. They were distressed by that and asked him to remove it from them and they would believe; but they did not. Each punishment would stay upon them for a week, and between one punishment and the next was a month. That is His saying ﴿آيَاتٍ مّفَصَّلاَتٍ﴾. Then Allah promised Moses that He would drown Pharaoh, so Moses travelled from Egypt by night. That reached Pharaoh and he pursued him — it is said with a million and a hundred thousand, besides the battalion he was in and his two wings — and he and his companions overtook them at sunrise. Moses struck the sea with his staff, and twelve roads opened for him in it. When they had come out, Pharaoh and his companions followed him in his road; and when the first of them was about to come out and the last of them was in the sea, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, closed it over them and drowned them. Then Moses's companions asked him that Pharaoh be brought out so that they might see him; so he and his companions were brought out, and they took of the goods and weapons that with which they made the calf.

farraa:137-137.t:
His saying: ﴿وَأَوْرَثْنَا ٱلْقَوْمَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَانُواْ يُسْتَضْعَفُونَ مَشَارِقَ ٱلأَرْضِ وَمَغَارِبَهَا﴾: you put مشارق and مغارب in the accusative meaning: in the easts of the land and in its wests, and you make (وأورثنا) fall upon His saying ﴿ ٱلَّتِي بَارَكْنَا فِيهَا﴾. Or you may make (وأورثنا) fall upon the easts and the wests, since they were made to inherit them, and make (التى) a naʿt (adjective) of the easts and the wests, so that it is accusative; and if you wish you may make (التى) a naʿt of الأرض, so that it is genitive.
His saying: (وما ظلمونا): He says: they did not diminish anything of Ours by what they did, but they diminished themselves.
The Arabs say: "ظلمت سِقاءك" when you give [the milk of] your skin to drink before it has been churned and its butter taken out. And one says: "ظلم الوادى" when the water reaches a place in the valley it had not reached in the past; one of them recited to me:
يكاد يطلع ظلما ثم يمنعه * عن الشواهِق فالوادِى به شِرق
(It almost rises beyond its bounds, then [something] holds it back from the heights, and the valley is choked with it.)
And one says: "he is more wrongful than a snake", because it comes to a burrow it did not dig and lives in it. And they say: "ما ظلمك أن تفعل", meaning: what prevented you from doing. And al-arḍ al-maẓlūma is land which the rain has not reached. Abū al-Jarrāḥ said: "ما ظلمك أَن تفِىء" ("what kept you from vomiting?") to a man who complained of eating too much. And one says: ṣaʿiqa the man and ṣuʿiqa when the thunderbolt strikes him; and saʿida and suʿida; and rahiṣat the beast and ruhiṣat.

farraa:148-148.t: His saying: ﴿عِجْلاً جَسَداً لَّهُ خُوَارٌ﴾: it was a hollow body. And it has come in the exegesis that it lowed once only.

farraa:149-149.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَمَّا سُقِطَ فِيۤ أَيْدِيهِمْ﴾: out of remorse. And it is said: أسقِط is a dialect form; but (سقِط فى أيديهم) is more common and better. ﴿قَالُواْ لَئِن لَّمْ يَرْحَمْنَا رَبُّنَا﴾: accusative as an invocation (لئِن لم ترحمنا ربَّنا), and it is read (لئِن لم يرحمنا ربُّنا). The accusative is dearer to me, because in the codex of ʿAbdallāh it is (قالوا ربَّنا لئِن لم ترحمنا).

farraa:150-150.t:
His saying: ﴿أَعَجِلْتُمْ أَمْرَ رَبِّكُمْ﴾: you say عجِلت الشىء: I outstripped it; and أعجلته: I urged it on.
His saying: ﴿وَأَلْقَى ٱلأَلْوَاحَ﴾: it is mentioned that they were two tablets. It is permissible to say "tablets" for two, as He said: ﴿فإنْ كان لَهُ إخْوَةٌ﴾, and they are two brothers; and as He said: ﴿إن تَتُوبَا إلى اللّهِ فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا﴾, and they are two hearts.
His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿قَالَ ٱبْنَ أُمَّ﴾: it is read (ابن أمَّ) and (أُمِّ), with the accusative and the genitive; that is because it is frequent in speech, so the Arabs dropped the yāʾ from it. They hardly ever drop the yāʾ except from the noun addressed in the vocative, when the speaker puts it in construct with himself — except for their saying "يا بن عمّ" and "يا بن أمِّ"; that is because these two are frequently used in their speech. When something comes that is not commonly used, they keep the yāʾ, saying: "يا بن أبى", "يا بن أخى", "يا بن خالتى", keeping the yāʾ. For that reason they said "يا بن أمَّ" and "يا بن عمَّ" with the accusative, as the singular is put in the accusative in some cases; so it is said "حسرتا" and "يا ويلتا"; as though they said "يا أمّاه" and "يا عمَّاه". They did not say that with أخ, but if it were said it would be correct. Aaron was his brother by his father and his mother; he said to him (يا بن أم) only to appeal to his tenderness towards him.
His saying: ﴿فَلاَ تُشْمِتْ بِيَ ٱلأَعْدَآءَ﴾ is from أشمت. Muḥammad narrated to us, he said: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us, he said: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us from a man — I think it was al-Aʿraj — from Mujāhid that he read (فلا تَشْمِت بى), and it has not been heard from the Arabs. Al-Kisāʾī said: I do not know; perhaps they intended (فلا تَشْمَت بِى الأعداءُ). If it is sound, it has parallels: the Arabs say فرَغت and فرِغت; whoever says فرَغت says أنا أفرُغ, and whoever says فرِغت says أنا أَفرَغ; and رَكَنت and رِكنت; and شمِلهم شر and شمَلهم, in much of the language. And (الأعداء) is nominative, because the verb belongs to them, for whoever reads تَشْمَت or تَشْمِت.

farraa:155-155.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱخْتَارَ مُوسَىٰ قَوْمَهُ سَبْعِينَ رَجُلاً﴾: the exegesis has come: he chose from them seventy men. The verb was allowed to fall on them when (مِن) was dropped only because it is taken from your saying: "هؤلاء خير القوم" and "خير من القوم" ("these are the best of the people"). Since the construct was permissible in place of (مِن) without the meaning changing, they allowed themselves to say: "اخترتكم رجلا" and "اخترت منكم رجلا" ("I chose a man from you"). The poet said:
فقلت له اخترها قَلُوصا سمِينة * وناباً علينا مثل نابك فى الحَيَا
فقام إليها حَبْتَر بِسلاحِهِ * فللّه عينا حَبْتَرٍ أَيَّما فتى
(I said to him: choose from them a fat young she-camel and an old she-camel of ours like your own old one in fatness. So Ḥabtar rose to it with his weapon — how admirable are Ḥabtar's eyes, what a youth!)
And the rajaz poet said:
* تحت الذى اختار له الله الشجو *
(Beneath the one for whom Allah chose the trees.)
His saying: ﴿أَتُهْلِكُنَا بِمَا فَعَلَ ٱلسُّفَهَآءُ مِنَّآ﴾: that is because Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent the quaking upon those who were with him — and they were seventy — and they were burnt. Moses thought they had been destroyed because their companions had taken the calf, so he said: "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?" But they were destroyed only because they asked Moses: (أرنا الله جهرة).
His saying ﴿ثم اتخذوا العِجل﴾ is not referred back to His saying ﴿فأخذتهم الصاعقة﴾ "then they took"; this is referred back to their first deed. There is another view in it: that you make (ثم) a fresh statement. The Arabs may begin anew with ثم while the verb after it took place before the first verb; of that is your saying to a man: "I have given you a thousand, then I gave you wealth before that"; so (ثم) is a conjunction on the report of the reporter; as though he said: I tell you that I visited you today, then I tell you that I visited you yesterday.
As for the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿خلقكم مِن نفسٍ واحِدةٍ ثم جعل مِنها زوجها﴾, this sense is in it; lest someone say: how did He say "He created you, then made from it its mate", when the mate was created before the offspring? So this explained sense covers this meaning. And if you wish you may make (ثم) refer back to "one" (الواحدة); He meant — and Allah knows best — He created you from a soul on its own, then made from it its mate; so (ثم) comes after His creating Adam alone. This is what there is in ثم. The natural character of ثم is that [what follows it] is later; and likewise the fāʾ. As for the wāw, if you wish you may make the last the first and the first the last. When you say "I visited ʿAbdallāh and Zayd", whichever of them you wish may be the one first visited; but when you say "I visited ʿAbdallāh then Zayd" or "I visited ʿAbdallāh, and so Zayd (فزيدا)", the first is before the last — unless by the last you mean it to be referred back to the report of the reporter, so that you make it first.

farraa:160-160.t:
His saying: ﴿وَقَطَّعْنَاهُمُ ٱثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ﴾: He said اثنتى عشرة (feminine), while al-sibṭ (tribe) is masculine, because after it comes أمم (nations), so the feminine went to the nations.
If it were (اثنى عشر), on account of the masculine al-sibṭ, it would be permissible.

farraa:163-163.t:
His saying: ﴿وَسْئَلْهُمْ عَنِ ٱلْقَرْيَةِ ٱلَّتِي كَانَتْ حَاضِرَةَ ٱلْبَحْرِ إِذْ يَعْدُونَ فِي ٱلسَّبْتِ﴾: the Arabs say يُسْبِتون and يَسْبِتون, and سَبَت and أَسبت. The meaning of أسبتوا is: they entered the Sabbath; and the meaning of يَسبِتون is: they keep their Sabbath. Similar to it in speech: "قد أجمعنا", i.e. a Friday has passed us; and "جَمَّعنا": we attended the Friday prayer. He said: and one of the Arabs said to me: "أترانا أشهرنا مذ لم نلتق؟" ("do you think a month has passed us since we last met?"), meaning: a month has passed us.
﴿وَيَوْمَ لاَ يَسْبِتُونَ﴾ is accusative by His saying: ﴿لاَ تَأْتِيهِمْ﴾.

farraa:164-164.t: His saying: ﴿قَالُواْ مَعْذِرَةً﴾: we did that as an excuse. Most of the speech of the Arabs puts al-maʿdhira in the accusative, but the Readers preferred its nominative; and its accusative is permissible. Whoever reads the nominative says: it is an excuse (هى معذرة), as He said: ﴿إِلا ساعة مِن نهارٍ بلاغ﴾.

farraa:167-167.t: His saying: ﴿مَن يَسُومُهُمْ سُوۤءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ﴾: the jizya (poll-tax), until the Day of Resurrection.

farraa:169-169.t: His saying: ﴿ فَخَلَفَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ وَرِثُواْ ٱلْكِتَابَ﴾ and ﴿خَلْف أضاعوا الصلاة﴾, i.e. a generation, with the lām quiescent. And al-khalaf (with fatḥa) is what you take as a replacement; you say: "أعطاك الله خَلَفا مما ذهب لك" ("may Allah give you a replacement for what you lost"), and "أنت خَلَف سَوْء" ("you are a bad successor") — I heard it from the Arabs.

farraa:170-170.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُمَسِّكُونَ بِٱلْكِتَابِ﴾, and it is read (يُمْسِكون بالكتاب); its meaning is: they hold to what is in it.

farraa:171-171.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذ نَتَقْنَا ٱلْجَبَلَ﴾: He raised the mountain over their camp, a parasang by a parasang. (نَتَقْنا): We raised. And one says "امرأة مِنتاق" ("a natāq woman") when she has many children.

farraa:176-176.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّهُ أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلأَرْضِ﴾: he inclined to it and settled. And in a dialect form one says خلد إلى الأرض without alif, but it is rare.
And it is said of a man when the black of his hair and beard remains: "he is mukhlid"; and when his teeth do not fall out it is said: "he is indeed mukhlid".

farraa:187-187.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيَّانَ مُرْسَاهَا﴾: al-mursā is in the position of the nominative.
﴿ثَقُلَتْ فِي ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَٱلأَرْضِ﴾: it is heavy for the people of the earth and the heaven to know it.
His saying: ﴿كَأَنَّكَ حَفِيٌّ﴾: "as though you were ḥafiyy about it" — placed earlier and later [i.e. the word order is inverted]; its meaning is: they ask you about it as though you were ḥafiyy with it. And it is said in the exegesis: "as though you were ḥafiyy", i.e. as though you had knowledge of it.

farraa:188-188.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ كُنتُ أَعْلَمُ ٱلْغَيْبَ لاَسْتَكْثَرْتُ مِنَ ٱلْخَيْرِ﴾: He says: if I knew the unseen, I would have prepared for the barren year from the fertile year, and I would have known of dearness and prepared for it in the time of cheapness. This is the saying of Muhammad ﷺ.

farraa:189-189.t:
His saying: ﴿حَمَلَتْ حَمْلاً خَفِيفاً﴾: the fluid is light on the woman when she conceives.
﴿فَمَرَّتْ بِهِ﴾: she continued with it: she stood up and sat down with it.
﴿فَلَمَّآ أَثْقَلَتْ﴾: when her delivery drew near, Iblīs came to her and said: "What is in your belly?" She said: "I do not know." He said: "Perhaps it is a beast; so what will you do for me if I pray to Allah for you until He makes it a human?" She said: "Say." He said: "You will name him with my name." She said: "And what is your name?" He said: "al-Ḥarth."
So she named him ʿAbd al-Ḥārith, and did not know that he was Iblīs.

farraa:190-190.t: His saying: ﴿جَعَلاَ لَهُ شُرَكَآءَ﴾: when she said "ʿAbd al-Ḥārith", whereas one ought to be a servant (ʿabd) of none but Allah. And it is read: "شِرْكاً".

farraa:191-191.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيُشْرِكُونَ مَا لاَ يَخْلُقُ شَيْئاً﴾: by (ما) He meant the gods, and did not say مَن; then He made their verb like the verb of men [i.e. the plural of rational beings].
And He said: ﴿وَهُمْ يُخْلَقُونَ﴾ and they do not possess [anything].
[Translator's note: the source has "وقل" ("and say"), evidently for "وقال" ("and He said").]

farraa:192-192.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾: He made the verb that of men [i.e. the plural of rational beings].

farraa:193-193.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِن تَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَى ٱلْهُدَىٰ﴾: He says: if the polytheists call the gods to guidance, they will not follow them.
His saying: ﴿سَوَآءٌ عَلَيْكُمْ أَدَعَوْتُمُوهُمْ أَمْ أَنْتُمْ صَامِتُونَ﴾: He did not say "أم صممتُّم" ("or you were silent").
Most of the speech of the Arabs is on this: that they say "سواء علىّ أقمت أم قعدت" ("it is the same to me whether you stood or sat"). And it is permissible to say "سواء علىَّ أقمت أم أنت قاعد" ("… whether you stood or you are sitting"); the poet said:
سواء إذا ما أصلح الله أمرهم * علينا أَدَثْرٌ ما لُهُم أم أَصارِم
(It is the same to us, once Allah sets their affairs right, whether their wealth is abundant or they have but small herds.)
And al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
سواء عليك النفْرُ أم بِتَّ ليلة * بِأهل القِباب مِن نُميرِ بنِ عامِرِ
(It is the same to you whether you depart or spend a night with the people of the domed tents of Numayr ibn ʿĀmir.)
And some recited it (أو أنت بائت). And (أو) is permissible in it because of his saying "النفر" (departing); for you say "سواء عليك الخير والشر" ("good and evil are the same to you"), and (أو) is permissible in place of the wāw because the meaning is conditional (jazāʾ); as you say: "اضربه قام أو قعد" ("strike him, whether he stood or sat"). So (أو) leads to the sense of generality, as the wāw does.

farraa:198-198.t:
His saying: ﴿وَتَرَاهُمْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ﴾ means the gods: that they are images that do not see. He did not say "وتراها" because they have bodies and eyes.
The Arabs say of a man who is near a thing: "he is looking (yanẓur) [at it]", while he does not see it; and dwellings "look at one another (tatanāẓar)" when they face one another.

farraa:201-201.t: His saying: ﴿إِذَا مَسَّهُمْ طَائِفٌ﴾: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī read (طَيْف), and it is a slight offence (al-lamam) and sin. ﴿فَإِذَا هُم مُّبْصِرُونَ﴾: i.e. they desist when they see clearly.

farraa:202-202.t: His saying ﴿وَإِخْوَانُهُمْ﴾: the brothers of the polytheists (يُمدُّونَهُم) draw them on in error, so they neither take heed nor desist. That is His saying: (ثم لا يُقْصِرُونَ), meaning the polytheists and their devils. The Arabs say: قَصُر عن الشىء and أقصر عنه ("he fell short of / desisted from the thing"). So if it were read (يَقْصُرون) it would be correct.

farraa:203-203.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا لَمْ تَأْتِهِمْ بِآيَةٍ قَالُواْ لَوْلاَ ٱجْتَبَيْتَهَا﴾: they say: why have you not made it up yourself? It is from the speech of the Arabs; it is permissible to say "he chose the thing (اختار الشىء)" and "this is his choice".

farraa:204-204.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا قُرِىءَ ٱلْقُرْآنُ فَٱسْتَمِعُواْ لَهُ وَأَنصِتُواْ﴾: He said: people used to talk during the prescribed prayer; a man would come to the people and say: "How much have you prayed?", and one would say: "Such and such." So they were forbidden that, and speech in prayer was prohibited when this verse was revealed.
